input.text: When you divide one integer by another integer in C, the result is also an integer: any fractional part is thrown away before you ever store it in a float. Your average is being computed with integer division, so values like 5/3 become 1 and then turn into 1.00. Think about how to make the division itself happen with floating-point values.

content.text: The failure comes from integer division: the average is calculated as `sum / n` where both are integers, so the fractional part is discarded before the result is stored in the float. That's why values like 1.67 and 3.50 truncate to 1.00 and 3.00. The hint should point you toward performing the division with floating-point values instead.

input.text: The underlying issue is that integer division truncates toward zero. To keep the fractional part, at least one operand of the division must be a floating-point value before the division is performed. You can accomplish this by casting either the sum or n to float in the average expression — for example, convert the sum to float on the right-hand side of that assignment. That makes C choose floating-point division, and only then is the result stored in your float variable with the correct decimals.

content.text: The fix is to ensure one operand of the division is already a float before dividing, which makes C perform floating-point division and preserve the decimals. Casting the sum (or the divisor) to float in the average expression is the standard way to do this.
